The words

Drawn to the cross, which Thou hast blessed
With healing gifts for souls distressed,
To find in Thee my life, my rest,
Christ Crucified, I come.

Thou knowest all my griefs and fears,
Thy grace abused, my misspent years;
Yet now to Thee with contrite tears,
Christ Crucified, I come.

Wash me and take away each stain;
Let nothing of my sin remain;
For cleansing, though it be through pain,
Christ Crucified, I come.

And then for work to do for Thee,
Which shall so sweet a service be
That angels well might envy me,
Christ Crucified, I come.

How to sing it from the solfa

  • Find doh first. Play or hum Ab and sing d r m f s up from it, so the whole choir has the key in their ears before you start.
  • Pitch the first note. The tune starts on s, (E♭).
  • Count the time. 3/4 means three crotchet beats in each bar. In the grid every cell is half a crotchet: a dash (–) holds the note before it, and _ is a rest.
  • Know the notes. The tune uses d r m f s l t. A comma after a note (s,) is the octave below; an apostrophe (d') is the octave above.

About the hymn

Genevieve M. Irons wrote these words. They were printed in the Evangelical Lutheran Hymn-Book (St. Louis, 1927), as hymn 321.

The book printed the words without tunes, marked 8.8.8.6, to be sung to any tune of that metre. This page sets them to JUST AS I AM; any other 8.8.8.6 tune fits them as well.

  • Words: Genevieve M. Irons (1855–1928)
  • Music (1892): Joseph Barnby (1838–1896)

Questions about Drawn to the Cross, Which Thou Hast Blessed

What is the doh of Drawn to the Cross, Which Thou Hast Blessed?

In this version, in Ab major, doh is Ab. If your choir sings it in another key, doh moves to the new key note and every solfa syllable stays the same — that is what movable doh means.

What note does Drawn to the Cross, Which Thou Hast Blessed start on?

It starts on s, (E♭ in Ab major). Find doh first, then sing up or down to s,.

Is Drawn to the Cross, Which Thou Hast Blessed in the public domain?

Yes. Genevieve M. Irons died in 1928, Joseph Barnby died in 1896; the words were in print by 1927 and the music in 1892. Everyone named died before 1955 and both were published before 1929, so the hymn is out of copyright in the UK, the EU, the United States and Nigeria. Modern arrangements and translations can still be under copyright.
